description:
Team from Barcelona with backgrounds in engineering, chemical engineering and biology. We're interested in planetary science, Earth observation data and space exploration, and in how places on Earth can help prepare missions to the Moon and Mars.

https://aalexmc.github.io/analog-zero-2026-11-14
summary: Before a base goes to the Moon or Mars, it has to be rehearsed on Earth. Analog Zero is a web tool that says where, and when. Pick a world, a NASA mission objective and a month, then place a point: the tool compares every land cell of Earth on a 0.5° grid, not only the famous sites, with that point on eight measured parameters: terrain roughness, local relief, maximum, minimum and mean surface temperature, sunlight, vegetation, and rain and snow. Eight more exist only on Earth (dryness, mean and strong wind, day-night temperature swing, permafrost, elevation, rock type, travel time to a city) and are compared with NASA's own test site. An analog is a place and a month: for Jezero crater on Mars, the best match is in Canada over the whole year, in Mongolia in January and in Namibia in July. Each place shows what matches, by how much, and what Earth cannot reproduce: gravity and air pressure. Then one button rebuilds the whole base, piece by piece, on the Earth place and on the Moon or Mars point, on real terrain: habitat, landing pad, solar tower, fission reactor, water plant, rovers and drill, each checked against its published limits: OK, BREAKS or NOT MEASURED. A full day can be simulated hour by hour on both worlds, with the real Sun and the shadows of the terrain. A limit that is going to break should break here first. Every figure carries its source, and what we could not measure says so.
details:
What it does

Analog Zero is a website that runs entirely in the browser. You can try it here: https://aalexmc.github.io/analog-zero-2026-11-14/

You start by picking a world, the Moon or Mars, and then a mission objective. There are 21 of them, and each one is a kind of test that NASA already runs at analog sites on Earth, shown with the NASA campaigns behind it and a quotation from the source. You also pick a month, or the whole year.

Then you place a point. On the Moon the tool looks at the area NASA is studying, within 6° of the south pole, on real terrain. On Mars it applies NASA's published limits for a human landing zone.

Now the tool goes looking on Earth. It takes every land cell of a 0.5° grid (720 by 360 cells) and compares it with your point on eight measured parameters: terrain roughness, local relief, daily maximum, minimum and mean surface temperature, sunlight, vegetation, and rain and snow. For each place you see how far it is from your point on every parameter, in percent, and also what Earth can never reproduce, which is gravity and air pressure.

The last step is the rehearsal. "Generate simulation" puts the Earth place next to the Moon or Mars point at the same scale. "Generate base" lays out the surface systems of a lunar south pole base on both worlds, at the same offsets, and checks each piece against its published limits. The answer is OK, BREAKS (and by how much) or NOT MEASURED. The Sun of each world moves hour by hour and the terrain casts its shadows. "Generate report" puts everything into one file you can download.

What is new in it

For us an analog is a place and a month. The same place can be a good match in January and a bad one in July. For Jezero crater on Mars, the best place on Earth is in Canada if you take the whole year (81.7%), in Mongolia in January (85.8%) and in Namibia in July (83.3%). The Calendar tab tells you whether to stay or to move the test, and where to.

The tool starts from the mission and not from the map, so the mission decides which parameters count. The search also works backwards: give it the Earth site where NASA runs a test and it marks the spots A to E on the Moon or Mars that are most like it.

Instead of one winner the tool gives a portfolio, the smallest set of places that together cover every parameter. Whatever no place covers is sent to a lab. And the rehearsal happens on both worlds at once, with the same equipment and the same limits.

Benefits and intended impact

A team planning a field test can ask where on Earth, and in which month, an objective is best rehearsed. Before travelling they can see which limits of their equipment that place will stress and which it won't. Because the whole land surface is searched, places outside the usual list of analog sites show up. Students and the general public can use it too, since every screen has a Simple / In depth switch and an EN / ES switch.

How it works

For each parameter we take the difference between the Earth cell and the target as a percentage of a reference range. Similarity is 100 minus the mean of those differences over the parameters the mission uses. If either side has no data the result is "no data", never 0. Eight more parameters exist only on Earth (dryness, mean and strong wind, day-night temperature swing, permafrost, elevation, rock type and travel time to a city). Those are compared with NASA's own test site for that mission. We also group Earth's land into environment types using principal components and k-means, which is unsupervised and involves no trained model, and the tool warns you when a Moon or Mars point falls outside every type found on Earth.

Tools and languages

The website is plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with three.js for the 3D views. It has no framework, no build step, no server and no accounts, and it is published with GitHub Pages. The data pipeline is Python 3.12 with numpy, scipy, rasterio, pyproj and xarray, and it turns public NASA, USGS and ESA datasets into the files the website reads. We check the web with 738 automated tests (Node test runner) and 27 scripts that open each screen in a real browser with Playwright. No special hardware was needed, only our laptops.

About AI: we used Anthropic Claude through Claude Code to search and read sources, to write most of the code, tests and catalogues under our direction and review, and to review that code. Commits carry a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line. There are no AI-generated images or video. All pictures and clips are screen recordings of the app running on real data. The voice in the 30 second video is synthetic (ElevenLabs) and reads a script we wrote.

What we considered

We wanted to go beyond places that just look similar, so we compare measured layers and not pictures. An analog doesn't have to match everything, so we always show what matches, by how much and what doesn't, and we never give a verdict without its parts. Nothing is invented: every figure on screen carries its public source and the catalogue entries carry a literal quotation. Where a choice is ours, it is labelled "own rule" or "own metric". The limits of Earth as an analog are on screen as well, with gravity and air pressure shown as "cannot reproduce".

What it does not do

Similarity is not a probability. We fixed a validation of the global ranking before looking at the results, and it failed. Only 1 of 11 known analog sites fell in the best 5% for its key dimension, and we needed at least 8, so we keep the ranking as exploratory. There is no global layer for dust, subsurface, mineralogy, perchlorates or lava tubes, and those are shown as NOT MEASURED. The month only changes Earth, while the Moon and Mars keep their yearly value. Mars surface temperature comes from a reanalysis (OpenMARS) and is not a direct measurement.

Code, sources and seven short clips are in the repository: https://github.com/AAlexmc/analog-zero-2026-11-14
